mainTopic: Coin loans after a coin change, and רבה's rulings exempting damage that takes nothing away (coin in the sea, effaced coin, slit ear, burned שטר)
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion about repaying a coin loan after the coin was changed. Repayment follows the real metal value, using the rate set by רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע: ten old coins for eight new ones. Then רבה gives a series of rulings where someone harms another person's property without really taking anything away, and each time he is פטור. Throwing a coin into the ים הגדול is exempt, because the coin is still there to pick up, but only in clear water and only if he never lifted it. Wiping the image off a coin by hammering it flat is exempt, but filing metal off makes him liable. Slitting the ear of someone's cow is exempt, since the cow keeps all its ordinary uses and most cattle never go on the מזבח anyway. רבא challenges each ruling, using sources about מעשר שני, a slave who is deafened, and work done with מי חטאת, and each challenge is answered. Finally רבה rules that burning someone's שטר is exempt, because he only burned paper, and רמי בר חמא begins an objection that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A market price drop does not reduce the debt
steps.stepSummary: This finishes the ruling about a coin loan: if produce got cheaper only because of the market, the borrower's debt is not reduced.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the produce got cheaper because of the market, we do not reduce the debt for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a ruling that began just before this: if prices dropped only because of the market, and not because of the change to the coin, the borrower pays the full amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is to tell apart two causes of a price drop. A drop caused by the coin change itself can affect what the borrower owes. A drop caused by ordinary market swings is irrelevant to the loan.

keyTerms.meaning: The market, or the market price

phrases.english: And if it became cheaper because of the market
phrases.notes: "It" is the produce. Its price dropped for ordinary market reasons, not because of the coin.

phrases.english: we do not reduce it for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided ruling begun before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A price drop caused by the market alone does not reduce the coin debt.

steps.title: But the new coin is worth more as metal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: the new coin contains more metal, so repaying with it gives the lender extra value.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the coin has gained value as a lump of metal!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling. Even if prices did not change, the new coin is heavier, so it would be worth more if melted down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the borrower repays the same number of new, heavier coins, the lender gets more metal than he lent. That looks like getting back more than he gave, which comes close to רבית.

keyTerms.meaning: A bar or lump of melted metal

phrases.english: But it has gained value as a bar of metal!
phrases.notes: If you melted the new coin down, it would give you more silver than the old one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling that the debt stays the same.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the borrower repays the same number of coins.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The new coin holds more metal, so paying the same count gives the lender extra value.

steps.title: Use the exchange rate of רב פפא and רב הונא
steps.stepSummary: Instead, follow the real case ruled by רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע: eight new coins are paid for every ten old ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, do it like the case that רב פפא and רב הונא son of רב יהושע ruled on, with the coins of אגרדמיס the Arab merchant: up to ten old coins for eight new ones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the objection by giving a practical way to repay. It points to a real case where two אמוראים set the exchange at ten old coins for eight new coins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אלא shows that the simple approach of paying the same number of coins is dropped. The borrower instead repays by the amount of metal, so the lender gets back exactly what he lent.

keyTerms.meaning: They acted in a real case, gave a practical ruling
An Arab, usually a traveling merchant

steps.whatToRemember: When a coin is made heavier after a loan, the borrower repays by the actual value of the metal (ten old coins equal eight new ones), so the lender gets neither more nor less than he lent.

phrases.english: Rather, like this case

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַב פָּפָּא וְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
phrases.english: of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua,
who acted in a real case
with the coins of Agardamis the Arab merchant:
up to ten for eight.
phrases.notes: Ten old coins were treated as worth eight new ones, so eight new coins paid off ten old ones.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי הָא דְּרַב פָּפָּא וְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection by changing how the repayment is calculated.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical revision: repay by actual metal value, not by the number of coins.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Repaying the same number of coins would be fine.
steps.terutzMaskana: Repay at the ratio of ten old coins to eight new ones.

steps.title: Throwing a friend's coin into the sea is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that someone who throws another person's coin into the ים הגדול is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: One who throws his friend's coin into the Great Sea is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבה rules that a person who throws someone else's coin into the sea does not have to pay for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is surprising, because it seems that the owner has lost his coin. The reason comes in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt, does not have to pay

phrases.english: Rabba said:
One who throws his friend's coin
into the Great Sea is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: הַזּוֹרֵק מַטְבֵּעַ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ לַיָּם הַגָּדוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about damage to coins.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Throwing another person's coin into the sea does not make the thrower liable to pay.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as permission to throw away people's coins. The ruling is narrow, and the next steps limit it to clear water and to a coin that was not lifted up.

steps.title: Why is he exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רבה's ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the thrower should be exempt. This sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling looks strange, since the coin seems to be gone. So the גמרא asks for the logic before moving on.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind רבה's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the thrower does not have to pay.

steps.title: The coin is right there; take it
steps.stepSummary: The thrower can tell the owner: your coin is lying in front of you, so go pick it up.
steps.simpleTranslation: He can say: It is lying in front of you; if you want, take it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason: the coin is not destroyed, only moved, and the owner can still get it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damage means the item is ruined or lost. Here the coin is whole and can still be reached, so the thrower has not caused a loss he must pay for.

keyTerms.meaning: It is lying in front of you

phrases.english: He can say: Here it is, lying in front of you;
if you want, take it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of why he is exempt.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The coin is not lost; the owner can still retrieve it.

steps.title: Only in clear water, not murky water
steps.stepSummary: The exemption applies only when the water is clear and the coin can be seen. In murky water the thrower is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only in clear water, where he can see it. But in murky water, where he cannot see it, it does not apply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits רבה's ruling: it holds only if the owner can actually see his coin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason was "it is in front of you, take it." If the coin cannot be seen, that reason falls away, because the coin really is lost to the owner.

phrases.english: And this applies only in clear water,
where he can see it,
but in murky water,
where he cannot see it, no.
phrases.notes: "No" means the exemption does not apply, so the thrower must pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the ruling based on its own reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption holds only when the coin can be seen.

steps.title: Only if rolled in, not if picked up
steps.stepSummary: The exemption holds only if he pushed the coin into the sea without lifting it. If he picked it up, he became a גזלן and must return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only when he rolled it in. But if he picked it up in his hand, he has stolen it and must return it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second limit: lifting the coin is an act of stealing, which brings an obligation to return it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Picking up an item is a קנין, so lifting the coin makes him a גזלן. A גזלן has the duty of השבה, giving the item back into the owner's hand, and leaving it in the sea does not do that.

keyTerms.meaning: He just rolled or pushed it along
Returning a stolen item to its owner

phrases.english: And this applies only when he rolled it along,
but if he picked it up in his hand,
he has stolen it,
and he must perform returning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second limit to the exemption.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If he lifted the coin, he is a גזלן and must actually return it.
steps.whatToRemember: רבה's exemption needs two things: the coin can be seen (clear water), and the thrower never lifted it (only rolled it in).

steps.title: רבא challenges from the laws of מעשר שני
steps.stepSummary: רבא cites a ברייתא: money that fell into the ים הגדול cannot be used to redeem מעשר שני. This suggests such money counts as lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected: We do not redeem on money that is not in one's possession. How so? If he had money in a fortress, or in הר המלך, or his purse fell into the Great Sea, we do not redeem.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רבה's ruling with a ברייתא that treats money in the sea as out of the owner's possession.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If money in the sea is not "in his possession" for מעשר, it seems to be lost. Then throwing a coin into the sea should count as causing a loss, and the thrower should have to pay.

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection:
We do not redeem onto money
phrases.notes: This is about redeeming מעשר שני, moving its holiness onto coins.

phrases.english: that is not in his possession.
How so?
If he had money in a fortress,
or in the King's Mountain,
or his purse fell into the Great Sea,
we do not redeem!

steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's claim that a coin in the sea is not lost.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא treats money in the sea as out of one's possession, which suggests it is lost.

steps.title: מעשר is different: it must be in your hand
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that מעשר has a special requirement that the money be in your hand. Money in the sea fails that test, but it is still not lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: מעשר is different, because we need it to be available in your hand, as the Torah says: "and bind up the money in your hand," and that is missing here.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה defends his ruling. The rule for מעשר comes from a special פסוק and says nothing about whether the money is lost.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Redeeming מעשר requires money that is physically "in your hand" (דברים 14:25). Money in the sea fails that extra requirement, but it still belongs to the owner and can be retrieved, so for damages it is not lost.
steps.whatToRemember: Money in the sea is "not in your hand" for redeeming מעשר, but it is still not considered lost for damages. So רבה's exemption stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a special Torah requirement for one מצוה does not define a general idea like loss for other areas of halacha.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
It is different regarding tithe,
because we need it to be available in your hand,
as the Merciful One said:
"And bind up the money in your hand,"
and that is not the case here.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: מעשר has a special "in your hand" requirement from a פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Money in the sea counts as lost, so the thrower should pay.
steps.terutzMaskana: Money in the sea fails only the special מעשר requirement; it is not lost, so the thrower stays exempt.

steps.title: Rubbing smooth a friend's coin is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that one who rubs off the image of another person's coin is פטור, because he did nothing to the coin itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה said: Someone who rubs smooth his friend's coin is exempt. Why? Because he didn't really do anything to it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a new ruling about another kind of damage that leaves the object itself in place. Someone wipes the image off a coin, and רבה says he does not have to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The coin may no longer be usable as money, so its owner loses value. Still, רבה says the metal is all there and nothing was taken away, so nothing counts as damage. This fits the earlier steps, where the coin pushed into the sea was also not treated as lost.

keyTerms.meaning: Rubs or smooths down, here meaning wiping the image off a coin
Exempt, does not have to pay
He did not do anything at all

phrases.english: And Rabba said:
One who rubs smooth his friend's coin is exempt.
phrases.notes: He wipes off the stamped image, so the coin can no longer be spent as money.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Because he did not do anything at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה: הַשָּׁף מַטְבֵּעַ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling by רבה, joined to his earlier ruling about the coin pushed into the sea
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rubbing the image off another's coin is exempt, because nothing was taken away from the coin itself (לא עבד ולא מידי).

steps.title: Limit: hammering is exempt, filing is liable
steps.stepSummary: The exemption applies only when he flattened the coin with a hammer. If he filed it down, he actually made it smaller and must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only when he hit it with a hammer and flattened it. But if he filed it with a file, he really took some of it away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows רבה's ruling. Hammering is exempt, but filing is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hammering moves the metal around, but all of the metal stays there. Filing scrapes metal off, so the coin really is smaller, and that is real damage he must pay for.

keyTerms.meaning: And these words apply only when, a phrase that limits a ruling
A file, a tool for scraping metal

steps.whatToRemember: For רבה, damage to a coin counts only when the coin itself is physically reduced, meaning metal is taken away. Changing its shape or lowering its value alone is not enough.

phrases.english: And these words apply
where he struck it with a hammer and flattened it,
but if he filed it with a file –
he actually made it smaller.
phrases.notes: So in that case he must pay, because metal was really taken away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the exemption from step 11 to flattening, not filing
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Flattening the coin with a hammer is exempt. Filing it down reduces it, so he is liable.

steps.title: Challenge from a slave who is deafened
steps.stepSummary: רבא cites a ברייתא: a slave goes free if his master blinds or deafens him. Deafening leaves no visible change, yet it still counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected: If a master hit his slave on the eye and blinded it, or on the ear and deafened it, the slave goes free. If he hit near the eye and the slave can't see, or near the ear and he can't hear, the slave does not go free.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רבה's ruling using a ברייתא about a slave who goes free when his master injures him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the ear is deafened, it looks exactly the same from the outside, yet the ברייתא treats it as a real injury. So damage should count even without a visible physical change, and the person who flattens a coin should have to pay.
steps.confusionAlert: The proof comes only from the first case, where he hit the ear itself. The second case, hitting near the ear, is a different issue and is not what רבא is relying on.

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection:
If he struck him on his eye and blinded it,
on his ear and deafened it –
phrases.notes: Some versions say וחרשו, "deafened him." The corrected wording in square brackets says וחרשה, "deafened it," meaning the ear.

phrases.english: a slave goes free because of these.
If he struck near his eye and he cannot see,
near his ear and he cannot hear –
a slave does not go free because of these.

steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling that flattening a coin is exempt because nothing physically changed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Deafening shows no outward change, yet the ברייתא counts it as an injury. So damage without a visible change should still count.

steps.title: Deafening always makes a real wound
steps.stepSummary: רבה holds elsewhere that deafening always causes bleeding inside the ear, so it is a real physical injury. That makes it unlike the flattened coin.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה follows his own reasoning, for רבה said: One who deafens his father is put to death, since deafening is impossible without a wound, because a drop of blood falls into his ear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבה by pointing to another ruling of his, which shows that he sees deafening as a real physical injury.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה holds that deafening always makes a drop of blood fall inside the ear, even if no one sees it. So the deafened slave was physically harmed, while the flattened coin lost nothing at all. The ברייתא does not contradict רבה.

keyTerms.meaning: Following his own reasoning (shown in another ruling)
A wound or bruise that draws blood

steps.whatToRemember: An injury can count even if it can't be seen from outside, as long as something really changed physically. Deafening is that kind of injury. Flattening a coin is not.

phrases.english: Rabba follows his own reasoning,
for Rabba said:
One who deafens his father is put to death;
since deafening is impossible without a wound,
because a drop of blood falls into his ear.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: deafening involves a hidden physical wound, while flattening a coin involves no physical change
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Deafening seemed to be damage with no physical change at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: Deafening always makes a hidden wound, so it is real physical damage. The coin case stays exempt.

steps.title: Slitting a friend's cow's ear is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that one who slits the ear of another's cow is פטור. The cow is as useful as before, and most cattle are never brought to the מזבח anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה said: Someone who slits the ear of his friend's cow is exempt. Why? The cow stays just as it was, since he didn't really do anything; and not all oxen are meant for the altar.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives another ruling along the same lines. Slitting a cow's ear, which makes it unfit to be a קרבן, does not require payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cow can still plow, give milk, and be eaten, so its normal uses are the same. The only loss is that it can't go on the מזבח, and since most animals are never brought as קרבנות anyway, that does not count as a loss.

keyTerms.meaning: It stands as it stood, unchanged

steps.whyThisMatters: This rounds out רבה's approach: losing a special, uncommon use, or losing value without a real loss, does not obligate payment.

phrases.english: And Rabba said:

phrases.aramaic: הַצּוֹרֵם אוֹזֶן פָּרָתוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: One who slits the ear of his friend's cow is exempt.
phrases.notes: A slit ear is a blemish, so the cow can no longer be brought as a קרבן.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
The cow stands just as it stood,
since he did not do anything;

phrases.aramaic: וְכוּלְּהוּ שְׁווֹרִים לָאו לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ קָיְימִי.
phrases.english: and not all oxen stand ready for the altar.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה: הַצּוֹרֵם אוֹזֶן פָּרָתוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another ruling by רבה with the same reasoning as the coin case
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Slitting another's cow's ear is exempt, because the cow is unchanged for normal use and most cattle are not meant for the מזבח.

steps.title: רבא challenges from work done with the red heifer and its water
steps.stepSummary: רבא brings a ברייתא: one who does work with מי חטאת or פרת חטאת is פטור in human court but חייב in the Heavenly court. He reads it as saying this is only because the damage is invisible, so slitting a cow's ear, which is visible, should be חייב in human court. That goes against רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected: "One who does work with the water of purification or with the red heifer is exempt in human court but liable in the Heavenly court." That exemption must be because work leaves no noticeable damage. But slitting the ear, where the damage can be seen, should make him liable in human court!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רבה's ruling from step 15 that slitting another's cow's ear is פטור. He uses a ברייתא to argue that visible damage should make a person pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Doing work with מי חטאת or פרת חטאת ruins them for their use, but you can't see any change in them. The ברייתא says this is פטור in human court. רבא reasons that the exemption depends on the damage being invisible, so slitting an ear, which can be seen, should be חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: the purification water mixed with the ashes of the red heifer
the red heifer, whose ashes are used for purification
liability in a human court / liability in the Heavenly court
its damage is noticeable or visible

steps.confusionAlert: Doing work with these items does not change how they look. It only makes them unfit for their holy use. That is why it counts as damage you cannot see.

phrases.english: Rava raises an objection:
One who does work with the water of purification
phrases.notes: Doing work with this water makes it unfit for purifying, even though nothing about it looks different.

phrases.english: or with the red heifer of purification
is exempt by human courts,
but liable by the laws of Heaven.
It is work whose damage is not noticeable [that is exempt];
but slitting [the ear], whose damage is noticeable,
phrases.notes: This is רבה's case from before: slitting the ear of someone else's cow.

phrases.english: would indeed be liable by human courts!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's exemption for slitting a cow's ear in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling that one who slits another's cow's ear is פטור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא exempts work with מי חטאת only because the damage is invisible. So visible damage like slitting should be חייב in human court.

steps.title: Slitting is also exempt; the ברייתא teaches Heavenly liability
steps.stepSummary: The answer: slitting is also פטור in human court. The ברייתא chose the invisible-damage case to teach that even when nothing can be seen, a person is still חייב בדיני שמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: the same is true that even one who slits is exempt. The ברייתא is teaching us that even work whose damage is not noticeable makes a person liable in the Heavenly court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבה. It says the ברייתא never meant that visible damage makes you pay. It chose an invisible case for a different reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא read the ברייתא's case as limiting the exemption. The answer flips the point: the ברייתא picked the 'weakest' kind of damage to show that even that brings Heavenly liability. Slitting stays פטור in human court, so רבה's ruling stands.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what it comes to teach us

phrases.english: They say:
The same is true: even one who slits is exempt,
and this is what it teaches us:
that even work
whose damage is not noticeable
is liable by the laws of Heaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: הוּא הַדִּין דַּאֲפִילּוּ צוֹרֵם פָּטוּר
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the purpose of the ברייתא's case (a 'לא מיבעיא' style reading)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא chose invisible damage to show that only invisible damage is exempt in human court.
steps.terutzMaskana: Slitting is also exempt. The ברייתא chose invisible damage to show that even it brings liability in the Heavenly court.
steps.whatToRemember: For רבה, damage that neither reduces the object itself nor harms its ordinary uses (like slitting a cow's ear) is פטור in human court, but the person can still be חייב בדיני שמים.

steps.title: Burning another's promissory note is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that one who burns his fellow's שטר is פטור. He can say: I only burned your paper.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה said: One who burns another person's promissory note is exempt, because he can say to him, "I burned your paper."
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a new ruling in the same theme: damage that is not physical. Burning a loan document is פטור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The real loss is that the lender can no longer prove the loan. But the burner only destroyed a piece of paper, which is worth almost nothing. The loss of the proof is only indirect, so he does not pay for it.

keyTerms.meaning: a legal document, here a promissory note proving a loan

phrases.english: And Rabba said:
One who burns his fellow's promissory note is exempt.
For he can say to him:
I burned your paper.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה: הַשּׂוֹרֵף שְׁטָרוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another ruling of רבה in the same series about damage that is not physical (after the coin and the cow's ear).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who burns another's שטר is פטור, since he only destroyed paper.
steps.whyThisMatters: This raises the basic question of whether causing someone to lose the ability to collect money counts as damage you must pay for.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא asks what case רבה means
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא opens an objection to רבה's ruling by asking what exactly the case is. The full challenge comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא objected to it: What are the circumstances?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. רמי בר חמא starts to attack the ruling about burning a שטר by asking for the exact case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word מתקיף shows this is a challenge, not just a friendly question. Asking 'what are the circumstances' sets up a dilemma: the ruling may be hard to explain in whatever case we pick.

keyTerms.meaning: what are the circumstances? what case is this?

phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama objects to it:
What are the circumstances?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a challenge to רבה's ruling in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling that burning another's שטר is פטור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By asking for the exact case, רמי בר חמא prepares to show that in any realistic case the ruling is hard to accept. The details continue on the next amud.
